migrationNotes: Spine: stand at one pond and follow the food. Read the arrows, find where every route begins, push a change along the arrows, then ask what the arrows leave out: matter that goes round, energy that goes through, and the sizes they cannot show.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-reading-food-webs-1 and -why-start. The arrow direction is taught on the first screen and tested in the skill check (-7); the reason routes start at producers is taught on the third screen.

lesson.title: Follow the food

lead.text: The pond has a simple chain of feeding: the zooplankton eat the algae, and the small fish eat the zooplankton. Ecologists draw each of these links as an arrow that points from the food to the organism that eats it, so Algae → Zooplankton says that the zooplankton eat the algae. The arrow shows the way the food, and the energy in it, travels. Check the direction every time, because the arrow points towards the eater.

Real habitats are tangled. The heron eats small fish, and it also eats zooplankton directly, so two arrows end at the heron. A diagram that shows every feeding link in a habitat is a food web. The pond with all the living things in it and the surroundings they depend on is an ecosystem, and a food web is a map of the feeding in it. The arrows that end at an organism show its direct food sources.

afterFigure.text: The figure draws the pond web. Look at the heron: arrows from Small fish and from Zooplankton both end there, so it has two direct food sources. The small fish have only one, because a single arrow reaches them.

lead.text: Count the arrows that end at the hawk.

Trace any route backwards along the arrows and you always end at the same sort of organism. The algae are not eating anything. They make their own food, using light, in the way a leaf cell does. An organism that makes its own food is called a producer. In a meadow the grass is the producer, and in the pond it is the algae.

Every other organism has to eat. Zooplankton, small fish and herons are consumers, which get their food by eating other organisms. The producers are the only ones that bring new food into the web, so every route starts at a producer, no matter how long it is. The heron's meal of small fish traces back to zooplankton, and the zooplankton to algae.

afterFigure.text: That makes the producers the foundation of the web. If they disappeared, every consumer would lose its food sooner or later, whatever the web looked like in between.

lead.text: Look for the organism that does not need to eat anything.

steps.headline: A change moves along the arrows

lead.text: Because the organisms are linked, a change in one passes to its neighbours. Look at the arrow Zooplankton → Small fish. If the small fish were removed, fewer zooplankton would be eaten, so the zooplankton would tend to increase. If the zooplankton fell in number instead, there would be less food for the small fish, so they would tend to decrease. A change travels in both directions along an arrow: towards the eaters, which lose food, and towards the food, which is eaten less.

Webs are never quite that simple. The heron has two sources of food, so when the zooplankton decline it still has small fish to eat. Many animals can switch to other foods. A diagram tells you which links exist and which way a change is likely to push. It does not tell you how big the effect will be.
Zooplankton eat algae. Use that arrow to decide which way the loss of the zooplankton pushes the algae.

steps.headline: Matter goes round, energy goes through

lead.text: The arrows leave out what happens when an organism dies. A dead heron does not stay as it is. Decomposers, mostly bacteria and fungi, feed on dead organisms and waste, and in doing so they return the matter in them to the soil and the water as simple substances. Producers take those substances up again and build them into new tissue. Some of the atoms in the algae today may once have been part of a heron. Matter goes round in a cycle.

Energy behaves differently. Producers capture it from light, and each step along an arrow passes some of it on, but at every step much of it escapes as heat that no organism can use again. Energy is never cycled back. It flows through the ecosystem, which is why a pond needs a steady supply of sunlight to keep going, while the matter in it can be used over and over.
Think about what happens to energy at each step along the arrows.
Think about what the arrows of a small web show and what they leave out.

lesson.orientation: Read feeding arrows and separate energy flow from recycled matter.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Stand at the edge of a pond on a still summer day. The water is faintly green, because it is full of microscopic algae. Among them swim tiny animals called zooplankton, which feed on the algae. Small fish swim through the zooplankton and eat them, and now and then a heron wades in and eats the small fish.

Everything in the pond is tied together by who eats whom. Suppose a disease sweeps through and kills most of the zooplankton. The loss will not stay with the zooplankton. It will spread to the animals that eat them, to the algae they eat and to the heron that wades in for fish, though it will not reach each of them in the same way.

This lesson learns to read a drawing of those links, with arrows that point from food to eater. It shows where every route in the drawing begins, how a change travels along the arrows and what the arrows leave out. By the end you can read the feeding in a habitat and say what moves round it and what only passes through.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the arrows of a food web and say which parts of an ecosystem are recycled and which are not.

recap.keyIdea: Arrows point from food to eater, and every route starts at a producer. Matter is recycled by decomposers, but energy flows through and disperses as heat.

blocks.text: You counted the direct food sources of a hawk and traced every route back to a producer. You followed a change along an arrow, and you saw why a diagram of links cannot predict an exact count.

recap.nextHook: Energy escapes as heat at every step along a route. The next lesson measures how much, and asks how much of a producer's energy is left by the time it reaches the top of the web.

questions.prompt: What does the arrow Grass → Grasshopper mean?
hints: Follow the direction of matter and energy transfer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrows run from food to consumer.

choices.label: Grass turns directly into a hawk

questions.onCorrect: The grasshopper eats the grass. An arrow runs from the food to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the arrow backwards. It points to whichever organism is doing the eating.
An arrow shows eating, not turning into another organism.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: Which organism makes its own food from light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae build organic matter using light; the other organisms consume other organisms.

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They build their own food, so all the other organisms depend on them.

misconceptions.feedback: Animals eat other organisms. The producer is the one that makes its own food.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web, a hawk eats mice and frogs. Frogs eat grasshoppers, which eat grass. How many direct food sources does the hawk have?
hints: Count the arrows ending at the hawk.
Do not count indirect food sources.
Ignore the grass and the grasshopper: the hawk does not eat them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two arrows enter the hawk: one from mouse and one from frog.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count only the arrows that end at the hawk.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every organism in the web. Count only those the hawk eats directly.
That includes organisms further down the routes. Count only direct links.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through ecosystems and becomes less available for further biological work. In what form does much of it disperse?
hints: Think about metabolic energy that is not passed into new biomass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy disperses as heat; atoms can be recycled through environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Energy flows through and spreads out as heat, so ecosystems need a steady input.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are recycled. Energy is not, and it spreads out in another form.

questions.prompt: In a meadow food web the number of mice goes down. Can the diagram give an exact future number of hawks?
hints: Check what the arrows actually show.

acceptedIdeas: No, other food sources and conditions also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A feeding web shows relationships, not a complete quantitative population model.

choices.label: Yes, arrows specify exact population changes
No, other food sources and conditions also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Arrows show who eats whom, not how many. Other food and conditions matter too.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show feeding links only. They give no numbers.
The hawk also eats frogs, so losing mice does not remove its food entirely.

questions.prompt: A pond web is a chain of algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron, plus one extra link where the heron also eats zooplankton directly. How many feeding links does the web have in total?
hints: Count the links in the chain first.
A chain of four organisms has one fewer link than organisms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain has 3 links, and the extra link makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Count the links in the chain, then add the shortcut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chain alone. Add the extra link.
That is one more than the web has. A chain of four organisms has three links.

questions.prompt: In a food web an arrow points from a rabbit to a fox. Which organism is the consumer?
hints: Which way does an arrow point?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The arrow runs from food to consumer, so the fox eats the rabbit.

questions.onCorrect: The fox. The arrow points to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow starts at the food. The rabbit is being eaten here.

questions.prompt: Which kind of organism returns matter from dead material to the soil and water so that producers can use it again?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decomposers return matter from dead material to environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Decomposers. They recycle matter, though energy is not recycled with it.

misconceptions.feedback: Producers use the recycled matter. Another group returns it.

questions.prompt: A disease kills most of the zooplankton in a pond, and the zooplankton eat the algae. What happens to the amount of algae at first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With fewer zooplankton eating it, the algae increases at first.

questions.onCorrect: It increases. Fewer eaters mean less algae is eaten, which is how links in a web connect.

misconceptions.feedback: The algae's eaters were killed. Less of it is being eaten, not more.

questions.prompt: Why do all the routes in a web trace back to a producer?
hints: Where does the first food in the web come from?

acceptedIdeas: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only producers make their own food, so every consumer's energy traces back to them.

choices.label: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
Producers are always the largest organisms
Producers eat all the other organisms

questions.onCorrect: Producers make their own food. Every consumer's energy comes from them, directly or not.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide it. Grass and algae are producers because they make their own food.
Producers are not eaters. The arrows run from them to the consumers.
